title: Reading and fasting
hook: Megillah on reading Esther; Taanit on fasts and rain

segments.voice: Yesterday, seder and sukkah: a hut you can feel and four cups for every table. Your line: laws of joy. Today, a scroll and a fast.

Say someone knows the whole book of Esther by heart. Every word, every name, every one of Haman's sons. On Purim night they stand up before the congregation, close their eyes, and recite it flawlessly. A beautiful performance. According to the Mishnah, it doesn't count. The tractate beside it has its own surprise: a public fast where an elder stands up in the town square and tells the crowd that the fasting isn't the point.
screen: `ESTHER, BY HEART.` → `IT DOESN'T COUNT.` → `THE FASTING ISN'T THE POINT.`

segments.voice: Reading and fasting. First, Megillah, the tractate of the scroll. On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read from a scroll, and the Mishnah sets the terms. Read it out of order, and you haven't fulfilled the duty. Read it from memory, and you haven't either. It has to be read from the written scroll, in order. But for people who speak another language, reading it in that language counts. Strict about the text, generous about the listener. Second, Taanit, the tractate of fasts. Much of it is about rain: when to begin praying for it in the autumn, and what a community does when the rains don't come. The answer is a series of public fasts. On those days, says the Mishnah, the ark is carried out into the town square, ashes are put on it, and the eldest among them stands up to speak. He reminds the crowd of the people of Nineveh, who fasted in the book of Jonah. The verse doesn't say God saw their sackcloth and their fasting. It says, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation, "And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." Works. Not the fast. The fast is the doorway, and the turning is the room. Third, the two belong together, and Esther shows why. Before she goes to the king, she asks the Jews of Shushan to fast for her. The fast comes first, then the brave act. Reading and fasting: both are real only when something actually changes.
screen: `FROM THE SCROLL, IN ORDER.` · `IN A LANGUAGE YOU UNDERSTAND.` · `GOD SAW THEIR WORKS.` · `ESTHER FASTS, THEN ACTS.` · then, large: `READING AND FASTING.`

segments.voice: Choose something short, a few verses of Esther, a psalm, a paragraph that matters to you, and read it aloud from the page, in order, slowly enough to hear every word. Then set it down, sit with your breath, and let one phrase you'd skipped before stay with you.
Reading and fasting. Megillah, the scroll read from the page in order, and Taanit, the fasts that point beyond themselves to changed works. Today's word.
Your line: reading and fasting. Both point past themselves, toward something that changes. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: On Purim, Jews gather to hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, often making noise at Haman's name; on public fast days, congregations add special prayers and the Torah reading for fasts.

options: The Mishnah says it must be read from the scroll, in order; from memory doesn't count.
Yes. The Mishnah prizes memory, so reciting it by heart counts even more.
Yes, if she recites it in Hebrew; in any other language it wouldn't count.
